theme: Unit 23 review, The Better Covenant, Hebrews
memoryText: For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin. Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Today there is no new reading. Today is for review and reflection on what you have learned in Unit 23.

Begin by memorizing the verse above if you have not already. Hebrews 4:15-16 is the gospel for the weary believer. It tells you three things about Jesus and one thing about you.

First, Jesus sympathizes. He is not a high priest who looks down at weakness with disdain. He has felt hunger, grief, exhaustion, betrayal, and temptation. When you come to him, you are coming to someone who understands.

Second, Jesus is without sin. He was tempted in every respect, yet he did not fall. This is why his sympathy is not that of someone who gave in. He felt the full force of temptation, more than any of us, because he never gave way. And because he is sinless, his sacrifice is acceptable and his priesthood is effective.

Third, Jesus sits on a throne of grace. The throne is the seat of a king and of a judge. But for those who are in Christ, it is a throne of grace. The one who sits there has already paid for our sins.

And the verse gives you your part: draw near with confidence. Not with arrogance, not with a sense of deserving, but with boldness that rests entirely on him. You will receive mercy for what you have done and find grace to help in time of need. Say it aloud. Carry it with you into every need this week.
unitRecap:
In Unit 23 you have traveled through the whole book of Hebrews, the sermon that shows how Christ fulfills everything the Old Testament promised. It began with a majestic sentence: God has spoken finally and fully through his Son, the radiance of God’s glory and the exact imprint of his nature. You saw that the Son is greater than the angels, who mediated the law, and that he became human to free us from the fear of death. You read the comparison with Moses, the warning from Psalm 95 against hardening our hearts, and the promise of a Sabbath rest that remains for God’s people.

You came to the center of the book: Jesus is the great high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses, who passed through the heavens, and who invites us to draw near to the throne of grace. You read the warning in chapter 6 and the anchor of God’s oath. You saw Melchizedek, the priest-king of Genesis 14, as the pattern for a priesthood that never ends. You read the better covenant promised in Jeremiah 31, the better sanctuary, and the better sacrifice. The blood of bulls and goats could not remove sin, but the blood of Christ has cleansed the conscience once for all, and the curtain has been opened by his flesh.

Along the way you paused to consider the Ascension, where Christ was enthroned at God’s right hand and began his priestly ministry of intercession, and the doctrine of church membership, where Hebrews 10:24-25 calls us to gather and stir one another up. You studied Psalms 95, 40, 110, and 22, each of which Hebrews draws on to show the voice of the Son. You walked through the hall of faith in chapter 11, where all of God’s people lived by promises they only saw from afar, and you heard the call in chapter 12 to run the race, looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith. Finally, you read the practical commands of chapter 13 and the benediction that sums up the book: the God of peace, who raised the great shepherd by the blood of the eternal covenant, equips us for his will.

The message of Hebrews can be stated in one sentence: Jesus is better, so hold fast to him.

reviewQuestions.question: How does Hebrews demonstrate that Jesus is better than angels, Moses, and the Levitical priesthood?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Look back over chapters 1 to 7. Choose one comparison (Christ and the angels, Moses, or the Levitical priests) and explain in your own words why he is better. How does this help you trust him more fully?

reviewQuestions.question: What is the relationship between the Old Covenant and the New Covenant?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Reread Hebrews 8:1-13 and 10:1-18. List two things the old covenant could not do and two things the new covenant does. Which of these matters most to you today?

reviewQuestions.question: What does it mean that Christ is our high priest after the order of Melchizedek?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Consider Genesis 14, Psalm 110, and Hebrews 5 to 7. Why does it matter that Jesus is both king and priest, and that his priesthood never ends? Write a few sentences on what this means for your prayers.

reviewQuestions.question: What does Hebrews 11 teach us about the nature of faith, and how does it point us to Christ?
reviewQuestions.prompt: Reread Hebrews 11:1-3, 11:39-40, and 12:1-2. In your own words, what is faith, according to this chapter? Name one person from the chapter whose faith you want to follow, and say how each of them points to Jesus.

prayerPrompts: Thank God for the book of Hebrews and for the Son it reveals.
Tell him which comparison of Christ meant the most to you.
Ask him to keep the unit verse before you.
